title: John Deere See & Spray targeted herbicide application
titleEn: John Deere See & Spray targeted herbicide application
fidelityNote: Figures are John Deere's published claims from the 18 September 2024 release, including the Iowa State University study as Deere cites it. This record does not re-audit acreage, gallons, or the study. The release's footnotes say individual results vary.
executiveSummary: See & Spray uses boom-mounted cameras and onboard processors to spray herbicide only where a weed is recognized. John Deere's 18 September 2024 release says customers saved an estimated 8 million gallons of herbicide mix on more than 1 million acres in the 2024 season, with an average 59 percent herbicide savings on corn, soybean, and cotton in the United States. Cameras scan over 2,100 square feet per second at up to 15 mph. Customers pay for the acres where the technology is used. A PM copying this pattern separates those published figures from a grower's own as-applied maps.
problemStatement: Broadcast spraying puts herbicide on crop and on bare ground, not only on weeds. That spends chemical, water, and stops, and it is a poor fit for a stewardship target. A camera system that cannot show where it sprayed leaves the grower with a vendor percentage and no field record.
opportunity: See & Spray, introduced in 2021, opens individual ExactApply nozzles when cameras and processors class a plant as a weed. Deere's release says the 2024 season covered corn, soybean, cotton, and fallow, and that an Iowa State University study it cites found 76 percent average product savings and 15.70 US dollars per acre economic savings on the study fields. In 2025 Deere said it would introduce an Application Savings Guarantee so customers pay for the technology when application savings are there.
strategicAlignment: Treat the machine as a measurement system as well as a sprayer. The Operations Center map is the evidence. The press percentage is the manufacturer's season claim.
businessValue: A grower or custom applicator can compare as-applied maps with a broadcast baseline on the same fields. The 59 percent and the 8 million gallons are Deere's 2024 season figures, not a promise for the next field.
regulatoryContext: USDA conservation program rules where relevant
deploymentModelLabel: On-machine cameras, processors, and nozzles, with Operations Center maps
architecturePattern: Boom cameras scan the crop, onboard processors class crop versus weed, ExactApply nozzles spray only the recognized weed, and John Deere Operations Center stores the as-applied map against a broadcast comparison.
planningBandNote: Amounts and durations below are planning bands for a similar program. They are not the publisher's result and not a price quote.

narrative.heading: What Deere published on 18 September 2024
narrative.body:
See & Spray, introduced in 2021, uses boom-mounted cameras. Onboard processors decide whether a plant is crop or weed and command individual ExactApply nozzles. The 18 September 2024 release says the system saved an estimated 8 million gallons of herbicide mix on more than 1 million acres in the 2024 season, equal in the company's comparison to 12 Olympic-sized pools over an area larger than Rhode Island. Average savings were 59 percent on corn, soybean, and cotton in the United States. Cameras scan over 2,100 square feet per second at up to 15 mph. The technology is described as available for corn, soybean, cotton, and fallow.

Customers pay for the acres where it is used. The release says that in 2025 Deere would introduce an Application Savings Guarantee so customers pay for the technology when there is an application saving. Deere also cites an Iowa State University study with 76 percent average product savings and 15.70 US dollars per acre on the study fields. Those are two different published figures. The release says individual results vary with field conditions, weed pressure, and settings.

narrative.heading: How a farm PM files it
narrative.body: Write a claim card with Deere's date, acres, gallons, and 59 percent. Run the season. File the maps. The farm's percentage is whatever the maps compute. Do not average the farm into the press release.
